guides.title: Redis or Kafka?
guides.dek: Both hold what you send them, and both get called "a queue". One is a very fast store for the present; the other is a log of what happened.
guides.intro: Pick by the job. If you need an answer in under a millisecond, reach for Redis. If several services need to read the same events, in order, and maybe read them again, reach for Kafka.

picks.title: Pick Redis when
items: You are caching, keeping sessions, counting for a rate limit, ranking a leaderboard or holding a short-lived lock with an expiry.
A command must take well under a millisecond, at around a lakh simple operations a second per node.
The data is small enough for memory, and losing about the last second of writes in a crash is acceptable.

picks.title: Pick Kafka when
items: Several services (notifications, analytics, search) each need to read the same events, independently.
You need events kept for days (7 by default) so a consumer can fall behind, or be replayed from any point.
Order matters per key, such as every event of one order, and the volume is very high.

table.label: Redis and Kafka side by side
head: Question
Redis
Kafka
rows: An in-memory store with data structures: strings, hashes, sorted sets, streams
A log of events kept on disk, split into partitions
Well under a millisecond inside one data centre
A few to a few tens of milliseconds with acks=all, in one region
As long as memory and your eviction policy allow; a failover can lose the last writes
7 days by default, with three copies
Plain pub/sub reaches only whoever is listening; streams add consumer groups, like a small Kafka inside Redis
Each consumer group reads everything, independently
Commands run one at a time on a single thread

example.title: At Zotato
paragraphs: Zotato limits each phone to a number of calls a minute. The count is a Redis counter with an expiry: INCR is safe without a lock because Redis runs one command at a time.

When an order is placed, the notification service, the analytics job and the search index each need to hear about it. The order service writes one event to a Kafka topic keyed by the order ID, so every event for an order stays in order, and each service reads it in its own consumer group. If notifications fall 7 minutes behind, the alert is consumer lag, and nothing is lost: the events are still in the topic.

guides.title: SQL or NoSQL?
guides.dek: The honest answer in an interview is "relational, unless there is a reason not to". Here is how to give the reason when there is one.
guides.intro: Start from the queries and the rules the data must keep, not from the name of a database. Reaching for an unusual database to sound clever invites questions you then have to defend.

picks.title: Pick SQL (PostgreSQL or MySQL) when
items: The data has relationships and you need joins and transactions: orders, payments, menus.
You want rules the database enforces, such as foreign keys and unique constraints.
One primary on good hardware is enough: thousands of writes and tens of thousands of reads a second, with read replicas and a cache for more reads.

picks.title: Pick NoSQL when
items: Wide-column (Cassandra) or key-first (DynamoDB): very high write rates, or data that arrives in time order, such as rider location pings and app events; you know the queries up front.
Document: records with varied shape that are read whole, such as a restaurant with its menu nested inside.
Key-value (Redis): a cache, sessions or counters always fetched by one id.

table.label: Which model for which job
head: Model
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Writes beyond one primary mean sharding, and cross-shard transactions are hard
Records read whole, with a varied shape
Changing one embedded dish rewrites part of a large document; data embedded in two places drifts
Caches, sessions, counters, one id at a time
No joins and few secondary lookups
Very high, steady writes, in time order
Queries that change often, and no joins or transactions
The same key-first model with no servers to run
Write the key schema for each access pattern first; a hot partition takes about 1,000 writes a second

example.title: At Zotato
paragraphs: Orders and payments live in PostgreSQL: an order and its payment change together in one transaction, and the restaurant's live-orders screen is one indexed query.

Rider location pings arrive every few seconds from every rider and are read as "this rider's recent locations". That is a wide-column or key-first table, partitioned by rider with a time bucket so no partition grows without limit. Menus are read whole, and cached in Redis. Each choice is tied to a requirement, which is what an interviewer wants to hear.

guides.title: Cache-aside or write-through?
guides.dek: Both keep a cache beside a database. They differ in who fills the cache and when a write is finished.
guides.intro: In an interview, say cache-aside unless you have a reason not to. Know the other two so you can say what the reason is.

picks.title: Pick cache-aside when
items: Reads far outnumber writes and only data someone asked for should be cached.
You are using Redis or Memcached, plain stores that know nothing about your database.
A little staleness is fine, and a TTL puts an upper limit on it.

picks.title: Pick write-through when
items: Reads must see fresh data right after a write, and you can afford slower writes: each write waits for the cache and the database.
You have a cache or framework that writes the database before it answers.
(Write-behind is a third choice: only for work where losing a few seconds of writes is acceptable, such as view counts and analytics events. Never for orders or payments.)

table.label: Three ways to write
head: Cache-aside
Write-through
Write-behind
rows: The database has it; then the cached entry is deleted
The cache and the database both hold it
The cache has it; the database gets it later, in batches
The first read of each entry, and every read after it expires, is a miss
Slower writes; data nobody reads again fills the cache
If the cache crashes before a flush, those writes are gone

example.title: At Zotato
paragraphs: A restaurant changes its biryani price from ₹240 to ₹260. With cache-aside the app updates the database and then deletes menu:42 from Redis, so the next reader fetches ₹260 and stores it. Delete, rather than update: two writers updating the cache in the wrong order can leave an old value there, while a delete can only cause one extra miss. A 10-minute TTL means a missed delete is at most 10 minutes out of date.

The "popular near you" list expires at 20:01:00, the dinner peak, and every request in that second misses. Coalescing fixes it: the first request takes a short lock and rebuilds the list, and the others wait or are served the old one. Dish view counts are written behind: losing a few seconds of them is harmless.

guides.title: WebSockets, polling or SSE?
guides.dek: Three ways to get one event to an open screen. The right one depends on who talks, how fast, and how many.
guides.intro: Say simple polling first, then improve it. Polling is a reasonable first answer, and it is good enough more often than people think.

picks.title: Pick polling when
items: The data can be seconds old: a delivery status refreshed every 10 seconds, a dashboard every minute.
You want plain HTTP, stateless servers and nothing special to run.

picks.title: Pick SSE when
items: Only the server talks: feeds, live scores, notifications, progress bars, answers streamed word by word.
You want the browser to reconnect by itself and tell the server the last event id it saw.

picks.title: Pick WebSockets when
items: Clients send often too: chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing.
You can run dedicated connection servers, because each connection is tied to one server.

table.label: Choosing
head: Who sends
Delay
Cost
Fits
rows: Status that can be seconds old; dashboards

example.title: At Zotato
paragraphs: A delivery's status can be 10 seconds old, so the app polls. Ten lakh phones polling every 5 seconds would be 2 lakh requests a second, mostly empty, so the interval matters.

The live score on match night goes one way, to crores of screens: SSE. Chat between a customer and a rider goes both ways: WebSockets, on dedicated connection servers. Whichever you pick, assume every connection drops: give each update a sequence number, send heartbeats, and reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, so a restart does not bring every client back in the same second.

guides.title: Queue or stream?
guides.dek: A queue hands each job to one worker. A stream is a log that many readers can read, and read again.
guides.intro: Ask what the message is. If it is a job to be done once, use a queue. If it is an event that several services care about, use a stream. Many systems use both.

picks.title: Pick a queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) when
items: Each message is a job, done once by one worker.
You want per-message retries, delays and dead-letter handling built in.
A spike must be absorbed for writes that can wait: analytics, notifications, search updates.

picks.title: Pick a stream (Kafka) when
items: Several services read the same events, each at its own pace.
You want replay from any point, order per key and very high volume.
A consumer that falls behind should catch up later, as long as retention (7 days by default) outlasts the lag.

table.label: Queue and stream
head: Question
Queue
Stream
rows: Built in, per message, with delays and a dead-letter queue
You build them: retry a few times, then park the event in a dead-letter topic

example.title: At Zotato
paragraphs: "Order placed" is an event: the notification service, analytics and search each read it from a Kafka topic keyed by the order ID. "Send this SMS" is a job derived from it: it goes on a queue, a worker takes it, and if the SMS provider times out it is retried later, waiting longer each time, and after the last attempt it lands in a dead-letter queue with its error for someone to look at.

If one worker dies halfway through a job, its lease runs out and another worker takes the job. Size the queue with the maths: (arrival rate − write rate) × the length of the spike, and check it drains before the next one.
